results.title: Neuroanatomy
results.question: What brain regions does the antennal lobe connect to?
results.response: The [antennal lobe](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003924 "Open antennal lobe in Virtual Fly Brain") is connected to various brain regions, including the mushroom body and lateral horn, through tracts and nerves. VFB records show that the antennal lobe projection neuron sends synaptic output to the mushroom body calyx and/or lateral horn. The connectome data indicates that there are tracts and nerves innervating the antennal lobe, and VFB holds [32](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003924,TractsNervesInnervatingHere "Run in VFB: Tracts/nerves innervating antennal lobe") records of these. VFB has annotated [676](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003924,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in antennal lobe") neurons with some part in the antennal lobe, and [673](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003924,NeuronsSynaptic "Run in VFB: Neurons with synaptic terminals in antennal lobe") neurons with synaptic terminals in the antennal lobe, which may provide further insight into the connectivity of the antennal lobe. To explore the connections of the antennal lobe in more detail, you can query the VFB database for neurons with presynaptic or postsynaptic terminals in the antennal lobe, or for parts of the antennal lobe.

results.title: Neuron characterisation
results.question: What is known about the LPLC2 visual neuron type? Where is it, what does it connect to, and what is its function?
results.response:
The LPLC2 visual neuron type is a lobula plate-lobula columnar neuron with a distinct dendritic arbor in each lobula plate layer, extending outwards from the main fiber in the direction of motion detection for the layer. Its cell body lies in the dorsal area of the lateral cell body rind. In the lobula, it has its main dendritic arbors in layers 4 and 5B, with minor processes in layer 5A, and presynaptic sites in layer 4. The arbors of LPLC2 cells span approximately 25 lobula optic columns, overlapping with other LPLC2 cells. LPLC2 projects to an optic glomerulus of the PVLP, anterior to LPLC1 and dorsal to LC4. The activity of LPLC2 elicits a jump escape response. There are approximately 80 of these cells per optic lobe and they are cholinergic. 

VFB holds information about the LPLC2 visual neuron type, including its structure, connections, and function, as described in publications by Wu et al. (2016), Klapoetke et al. (2017), Tanaka and Clark (2022), and Davis et al. (2020).

results.response: The organisation of the [antennal lobe](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003924 "Open antennal lobe in Virtual Fly Brain") in adult Drosophila has approximately 50 glomeruli, whereas in larval Drosophila it has around 22 glomeruli, indicating that the [adult antennal lobe](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00007401 "Open adult antennal lobe in Virtual Fly Brain") is more elaborated than the larval antennal lobe, as recorded in VFB. VFB holds various data related to the antennal lobe, including images, neurons with some part in the antennal lobe, and parts of the antennal lobe, with counts of [6](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003924,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of antennal lobe") images, [676](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003924,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in antennal lobe") neurons, and [100](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003924,PartsOf "Run in VFB: Parts of antennal lobe") parts, respectively. To further compare the organisation of the antennal lobe between adult and larval Drosophila, you can explore the available data, such as the [17046](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003924,ImagesNeurons "Run in VFB: Images of neurons with some part in antennal lobe") images of neurons with some part in the antennal lobe, or the [32](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003924,TractsNervesInnervatingHere "Run in VFB: Tracts/nerves innervating antennal lobe") tracts/nerves innervating the antennal lobe.

results.title: Bidirectional connectivity
results.question: Are there reciprocal connections between mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) and dopaminergic neurons (DANs)? Which pairs have the strongest mutual connectivity?
results.response:
The connectome data indicates that there are reciprocal connections between mushroom body output neurons and dopaminergic neurons. VFB records show 22 reciprocal class-level pairs between these two neuron types. The target-to-source weight is 7620 and the source-to-target weight is 2697, with 1102 target_to_source_pairwise_connections and 890 source_to_target_pairwise_connections. 

VFB holds downstream connectivity classes for [mushroom body output neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047953 "Open mushroom body output neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") ([2788](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for MBON") records) and upstream connectivity classes for [dopaminergic neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005131 "Open dopaminergic neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") ([7914](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005131,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for dopaminergic neuron") records), as well as upstream connectivity classes for mushroom body output neuron ([2077](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for MBON") records) and downstream connectivity classes for dopaminergic neuron ([8845](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005131,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for dopaminergic neuron") records). 

To determine which pairs have the strongest mutual connectivity, further analysis of the connectome data and the top_partners listed in the VFB findings would be necessary. VFB has annotated a large number of records for both mushroom body output neuron and dopaminergic neuron, including transgene expression and scRNAseq data, which could be used to inform this analysis.

results.title: Pathway tracing
results.question: Trace a pathway from olfactory receptor neurons to the lateral horn. What are the intermediate neuron types and their connections?
results.response:
To trace a pathway from olfactory receptor neurons to the lateral horn, we can look at the intermediate neuron types and their connections. According to VFB, antennal lobe projection neurons are intermediate neurons that connect olfactory receptor neurons to the lateral horn. The VFB-supported high-level pathway is [olfactory receptor neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005926 "Open olfactory receptor neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") -> antennal lobe projection neuron -> lateral horn.

VFB holds various data related to olfactory receptor neurons and the [adult lateral horn](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00007053 "Open adult lateral horn in Virtual Fly Brain"), including downstream and upstream connectivity classes for olfactory receptor neurons, and neurons with some part in, synaptic terminals in, presynaptic terminals in, and postsynaptic terminals in the adult lateral horn. 

For more specific information on the connections between these neuron types, you can explore the downstream connectivity classes for olfactory receptor neurons and the neurons with synaptic terminals in the adult lateral horn, as well as the tracts/nerves innervating the adult lateral horn.

results.title: Connectivity strength comparison
results.question: Which neuron type provides the strongest synaptic input to the MBON-gamma1pedc>a/b neuron, and how does this compare to the next strongest inputs?
results.response: The strongest synaptic input to MBON-gamma1pedc>a/b is from mushroom body intrinsic neurons, with a total weight of 45838, according to VFB data from the VFB query. The next strongest input is from Kenyon cells, with a total weight of 44880. This information comes from the VFB database. VFB holds a range of other data related to mushroom body output neurons, including downstream and upstream connectivity classes, which may provide further context for understanding the inputs to MBON-gamma1pedc>a/b.

results.title: Shared connectivity
results.question: Do the alpha/beta and gamma Kenyon cells converge on any of the same downstream MBON types? Which MBONs receive input from both?
results.response: The connectome data indicates that alpha/beta Kenyon cells and gamma Kenyon cells converge on the same [mushroom body output neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047953 "Open mushroom body output neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") types. VFB records show that there are shared downstream target classes among these source classes. According to the VFB compare downstream targets query, 13 shared downstream target classes were found among the compared source classes, suggesting that some mushroom body output neurons receive input from both alpha/beta Kenyon cells and gamma Kenyon cells. VFB holds extensive data on the downstream and upstream connectivity classes for mushroom body output neurons, with [2788](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for MBON") downstream connectivity classes and [2077](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for MBON") upstream connectivity classes annotated. To identify which specific mushroom body output neurons receive input from both alpha/beta Kenyon cells and gamma Kenyon cells, further queries can be made using VFB's downstream and upstream connectivity data for these cell types.

results.title: Anatomical containment chain
results.question: Trace the anatomical containment hierarchy from the DA1 glomerulus up to the top-level brain structure. What is each level in the hierarchy?
results.response:
The containment hierarchy from the [antennal lobe glomerulus DA1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003932 "Open antennal lobe glomerulus DA1 in Virtual Fly Brain") up to the top-level brain structure is: antennal lobe glomerulus DA1 -> adult antennal lobe -> adult deutocerebrum -> adult cerebrum -> adult central brain -> adult brain, as indicated by the VFB trace containment chain data. 

VFB holds data on the antennal lobe glomerulus DA1, including neurons with some part in it, synaptic terminals, presynaptic terminals, postsynaptic terminals, images of neurons, and transgene expression. 

To further explore the hierarchy, you can query VFB for more information on the adult antennal lobe, adult deutocerebrum, adult cerebrum, adult central brain, and adult brain.

results.title: Cross-region connectivity
results.question: What neuron types connect the central complex to the lateral accessory lobe, and how strong are these connections?
results.response:
The neuron types that connect the [adult central complex](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003632 "Open adult central complex in Virtual Fly Brain") to the [lateral accessory lobe on L3 CNS template, Wood2018](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_00050314 "Open lateral accessory lobe on L3 CNS template, Wood2018 in Virtual Fly Brain") include PFL1, PFL2_PB4, PFL3_PB7, PFL1_PB1, PFL1_PB7, and PFL1_PB2, as recorded in VFB. Additionally, VFB records show that larval mushroom body input and output neurons, and larval dopaminergic neurons, such as [larval dopaminergic DM1b neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00110928 "Open larval dopaminergic DM1b neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), [larval mushroom body input neuron l1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047968 "Open larval mushroom body input neuron l1 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [larval mushroom body output neuron c2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047964 "Open larval mushroom body output neuron c2 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [larval mushroom body output neuron f2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047974 "Open larval mushroom body output neuron f2 in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [larval mushroom body output neuron m1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047988 "Open larval mushroom body output neuron m1 in Virtual Fly Brain"), also connect the central complex to the lateral accessory lobe. 

VFB holds numerous records of neurons with some part in, or synaptic terminals in, both the adult central complex and the lateral accessory lobe on L3 CNS template, Wood2018, including [363](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003632,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in adult central complex") neurons with some part in adult central complex and [8](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=VFB_00050314,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in embryonic/larval lateral accessory lobe") neurons with some part in embryonic/larval lateral accessory lobe. However, the strength of these connections is not specified in the available data. 

To further investigate the connectivity between the adult central complex and the lateral accessory lobe on L3 CNS template, Wood2018, you can explore the available images of neurons with some part in these brain regions, including [13781](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003632,ImagesNeurons "Run in VFB: Images of neurons with some part in adult central complex") images of neurons with some part in adult central complex and [1404](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=VFB_00050314,ImagesNeurons "Run in VFB: Images of neurons with some part in embryonic/larval lateral accessory lobe") images of neurons with some part in embryonic/larval lateral accessory lobe.

results.title: Experimental planning
results.question: I want to study the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila. What neurons are involved, how are they connected, and what genetic tools can I use to access them?
results.response:
To study the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila, you would need to identify the specific neurons involved in this behavior. VFB does not currently hold data on the exact neurons involved in CO2 avoidance. 

The connectome data indicates that certain neurons in the antennal lobe and the ventral nerve cord are potentially involved in olfactory processing and sensory integration, which could include CO2 detection. However, without more specific information, it is unclear which neurons are directly responsible for CO2 avoidance.

VFB holds records of various genetic tools that can be used to access and manipulate specific neurons in Drosophila, such as GAL4 drivers and Split-GAL4 drivers. These tools can be used to express genes of interest in specific neurons and study their function. However, without knowing the exact neurons involved in CO2 avoidance, it is difficult to recommend specific genetic tools.

To further investigate the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance, you could query VFB for neurons that express specific receptors or sensors known to be involved in CO2 detection, such as the Gr63a receptor. You could also search for neurons that are connected to the antennal lobe or other regions known to be involved in olfactory processing. Additionally, you could explore the literature for studies that have investigated the neural basis of CO2 avoidance in Drosophila, which may provide more information on the specific neurons and genetic tools involved.

results.title: Complete neuron profile
results.question: Give me a comprehensive profile of the giant fiber neuron: its anatomy, connectivity, available driver lines, and relevant publications.
results.response:
The [giant fiber neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004020 "Open giant fiber neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") is a large adult descending neuron that controls jump escape behavior, as noted by Thomas and Wyman (1984). VFB records show that the giant fiber neuron has a distinct anatomy and connectivity. 

VFB holds [22](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of DNp01") records of images of the giant fiber neuron, which can be used to examine its anatomy. Additionally, VFB has annotated [14](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in DNp01") records of transgene expression in the giant fiber neuron, which may be useful for understanding its expression pattern and identifying relevant GAL4 drivers. 

The connectome data indicates that the giant fiber neuron has downstream connectivity classes ([361](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for DNp01") records) and upstream connectivity classes ([435](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for DNp01") records), which can be used to study its connectivity. 

For further information, you can explore the available images of the giant fiber neuron, examine its transgene expression, or investigate its downstream and upstream connectivity classes. Relevant publications, such as the one by Thomas and Wyman (1984), can provide more context about the giant fiber neuron's role in jump escape behavior.

results.title: Hypothesis generation
results.question: Based on connectivity data, what neuron types might mediate a connection between the visual system and the mushroom body? Could visual information reach the memory circuit?
results.response:
The connectome data indicates that neuron types such as [ML-VPN2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052139 "Open ML-VPN2 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mt-VPN1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052141 "Open Mt-VPN1 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mt-VPN](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052140 "Open Mt-VPN in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mti](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052142 "Open Mti in Virtual Fly Brain"), and T4ai might mediate a connection between the [visual system](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047735 "Open visual system in Virtual Fly Brain") and the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain"). VFB records show that adult visual projection neurons could also be involved in this connection. 

VFB holds numerous records related to the visual system and the mushroom body, including neurons with some part in these systems, synaptic terminals, and presynaptic and postsynaptic terminals. For the visual system, VFB has annotated [1046](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047735,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in visual system") neurons with some part in this system, while for the mushroom body, there are [602](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in mushroom body") such neurons. 

The available data suggests that visual information could reach the memory circuit, given the potential connections between the visual system and the mushroom body. To further investigate this, one could explore the specific tracts and nerves innervating the mushroom body, such as the [adult optic lobe-calycal tract](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00048333 "Open adult optic lobe-calycal tract in Virtual Fly Brain"), or examine the expression patterns overlapping with the mushroom body.

results.title: Comparative analysis
results.question: Compare the downstream targets of the two main types of clock neurons (s-LNv and l-LNv). Do they converge on any common target neuron types?
results.response: The downstream targets of [s-LNv](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch03yp "Open s-LNv in Virtual Fly Brain") and [l-LNv](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch0fws "Open l-LNv in Virtual Fly Brain") include several neuron types. According to VFB, comparing the downstream targets of s-LNv and l-LNv reveals 17 shared downstream target classes, including adult interneuron, adult cholinergic neuron, adult GABAergic neuron, adult glutamatergic neuron, adult octopaminergic neuron, adult dopaminergic neuron, and adult serotonergic neuron. This suggests that the s-LNv and l-LNv do converge on common target neuron types, such as adult cholinergic neuron. VFB holds data on these shared downstream targets, which can be further explored to understand the connectivity between these clock neurons and their target neurons.

results.title: Novel circuit exploration
results.question: What is the connectivity between thermosensory neurons and the mushroom body? Could temperature information influence memory formation?
results.response: The connectivity between thermosensory neurons and the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") is indicated by VFB downstream class-connectivity previews, which show that thermosensory projection neurons connect to mushroom-body-associated dopaminergic neurons and gamma main Kenyon cells. VFB holds extensive data on both thermosensory neurons and mushroom body, including downstream and upstream connectivity classes, subclasses, and expression patterns. For thermosensory neurons, VFB has annotated [430](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005918,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for thermosensory neuron") downstream connectivity classes and [263](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005918,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for thermosensory neuron") upstream connectivity classes. For mushroom body, VFB holds records of neurons with synaptic terminals, presynaptic terminals, and postsynaptic terminals in the mushroom body, as well as parts of the mushroom body and lineage clones found in it. The connectome data indicates that temperature information could potentially influence memory formation through the connections between thermosensory neurons and the mushroom body. VFB records show that thermosensory projection neurons have connections to gamma main Kenyon cells, which are involved in memory formation. However, the exact nature of this influence is not specified in the available data. To further investigate this, one could explore the specific connectivity patterns between thermosensory neurons and mushroom body neurons, such as the strength and direction of connections, using the available VFB data.

Genetic tools exist for SEZ neurons, as VFB returned 4205 genetic tool/expression pattern rows for the subesophageal zone, including GAL4 drivers and binary/intersectional drivers. 

To further explore the SEZ, you can query VFB for more information on its neuron types, connectomics data, and genetic tools. VFB has annotated N records for the SEZ, which can be accessed through VFB and VFB queries. The VFB query can also provide more information on the connectivity of the SEZ.
